title: 3 John

stories.title: 📜 3 John
summaryBullets: The elder, To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth: (1:1).
Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers. (1:2).
For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified about your devotion to the truth, in which you continue to walk. (1:3).
I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth. (1:4).
Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you. (1:5).
They have testified to the church about your love. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. (1:6).
For they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. (1:7).
Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth. (1:8).
I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction. (1:9).

So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church. (1:10).
Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God. (1:11).
Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true. (1:12).
I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink. (1:13).
Instead, I hope to see you soon and speak with you face to face. (1:14).
Peace to you. The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name. (1:15).
crossRefs: Romans 12:13 — Contribute to the needs of the saints, practice hospitality.
Matthew 10:40–42 — Whoever receives you receives me.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֹלֵךְ בֶּאֱמֶת (hōlēḵ beʾĕmeṯ) — Greek: περιπατοῦντα ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ (peripatounta en tē alētheía, NT) — Aramaic: מהלך בקושטא (mehaleḵ b-quštā)
translationNotes.note: Biblical idiom meaning to live one’s life in alignment with God’s truth, showing both belief and conduct.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַכְנָסַת אוֹרְחִים (hakhnāsat ʾōrḥîm, sense) — Greek: φιλοξενία (philoxenía, NT) — Aramaic: אושפיזא (ʾūšpīzā)
translationNotes.note: Hospitality was central in early Christian mission, enabling traveling teachers to be received and supported.

stories.keyTakeaway: John commends Gaius for walking in truth and showing faithful hospitality to brothers, urging support for such workers in the gospel.

intro:
3 John, like 2 John, is a short personal letter from 'the elder', the apostle John in his last years at Ephesus, likely in the 90s AD. The letter is addressed to a man named Gaius, an otherwise unknown believer who has been faithfully receiving and supporting traveling missionaries.

The letter has three short snapshots. First, John commends Gaius for his hospitality to brothers passing through, especially Gentile missionaries who have left home for the sake of the Name. Second, John warns against Diotrephes, a local figure who 'loves to be first' and refuses both to welcome traveling teachers and to receive John's own letters. Diotrephes apparently denies hospitality even to those Gaius would welcome and expels from the church those who do welcome them. Third, John commends Demetrius, who carries the letter, as well-spoken-of by everyone.

3 John is the New Testament's window into local church politics. A faithful man (Gaius), an ambitious gatekeeper (Diotrephes), and a trustworthy emissary (Demetrius); the kinds of figures every congregation has had. John promises to come deal with Diotrephes in person. The letter is short but pointed: pride in church leadership corrodes the body just as surely as false doctrine.
